summary: Defines a general framework for using assertions, which are signed statements issued by some other identity system, with OAuth 2.0. It adds a way for a client to authenticate to a token endpoint using an assertion, and a new authorization grant type based on one. Specific assertion formats are left to companion profiles.

eli5.summary: Instead of showing your own ID card, you show a signed note from someone the school already trusts. This document sets the basic rules for how a website can accept such notes to let you in.

questions: how to use assertions for oauth client authentication
subtitle: A common frame for letting OAuth 2.0 clients prove who they are, or what they may do, with a signed statement from someone else.

tldr.problem: OAuth 2.0 clients usually authenticate with a shared secret, and OAuth has no generic way to accept identity information issued by another security system.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC defines how a signed or MAC-protected assertion travels to the token endpoint, either as a client credential (client_assertion) or as an authorization grant (assertion), plus general rules for what an assertion must contain and how the server checks it.
tldr.outcome: It is only an abstract framework. Concrete formats come from companion profiles such as the SAML and JWT ones (RFC 7522 and RFC 7523), and deployments must still agree on identifiers, keys and lifetimes.

facts.label: Transport
facts.value: TLS required for token endpoint requests

today: RFC 7521 is a Proposed Standard from May 2015, and the metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. It is meant to be used together with a profile such as RFC 7522 (SAML 2.0) or RFC 7523 (JWT).

sections.title: Why Assertions in OAuth 2.0
sections.content:
In OAuth 2.0 (RFC 6749), a client gets an access token from an authorization server, usually by exchanging an authorization grant. OAuth lets new grant types be defined, which can serve as a bridge to other protocol frameworks.

This RFC uses that hook for assertions: packages of identity and security information that can be shared across security domains. It gives two uses. One is a client authentication method that does not send client secrets. The other is a grant type that helps in client-server integrations where the end user may not be present.

The two uses are separate. Client assertion authentication is only another way to authenticate to the token endpoint and has to be combined with some grant type to make a complete request. An assertion grant may be used with or without client authentication, and whether it is required is the authorization server's policy decision.
sections.eli5: A website normally lets you in with a password you share with it. This note explains a second way: bring a signed letter from someone the website already trusts.

sections.title: Assertions, Issuers and Relying Parties
sections.content:
An assertion typically says who the subject is, who issued it and when, and under what conditions it is valid, such as when and where it can be used. The entity that creates and signs it is the Issuer. The one that relies on it is the Relying Party, and here that is the authorization server.

Assertions in this framework MUST always be integrity protected by the issuer with a digital signature or a Message Authentication Code (MAC). They MAY also be encrypted, so that parties such as the client cannot read them.

The RFC describes two common ways to get an assertion. In the first, the client asks a third-party security token service, which mints and signs it. In the second, the client creates the assertion itself. A self-issued assertion can show knowledge of a secret, such as a client secret, without sending the secret, so it usually carries only a bare minimum of information.

The framework covers bearer assertions, which anyone holding them can use, so they must be protected in storage and transport. It is not directly suitable for holder-of-key assertions, which would need extra proof-of-possession mechanisms.
sections.eli5: A signed letter from a trusted teacher is a note anyone can carry, so you have to keep it safe. Sometimes you write the letter yourself and sign it with a secret stamp only you have.

sections.title: Sending Assertions to the Token Endpoint
sections.content:
All requests to the token endpoint MUST use TLS, because they carry clear-text credentials.

As an authorization grant, the request carries grant_type (REQUIRED; the assertion format, as an absolute URI), assertion (REQUIRED) and optionally scope. The requested scope MUST be equal to or less than the scope originally granted, and the server MUST limit the issued token the same way. Since the assertion is usually short lived, servers SHOULD NOT issue access tokens that outlive it by a significant period, so refresh tokens are usually not issued.

As client authentication, the request carries client_assertion_type (REQUIRED, an absolute URI) and client_assertion (REQUIRED). The client_id is optional because the assertion's subject identifies the client; if present it MUST identify the same client. A token endpoint tells assertion credentials from others by the presence of these two parameters.

An invalid or expired grant assertion gets the invalid_grant error. An invalid client assertion, or more than one client authentication mechanism, gets invalid_client.
sections.eli5: There are two boxes on the form at the front desk. One box holds a note that says what you may do. The other holds a note that proves who you are.

sections.title: What an Assertion Must Contain
sections.content:
The RFC defines an abstract metamodel: Issuer, Subject, Audience, Issued At, Expires At and Assertion ID. Profiles map these onto real formats.

  • The assertion MUST contain an Issuer. If it is self-issued, the Issuer MUST be the client's client_id.
  • It MUST contain a Subject. When the client acts for itself, the Subject MUST be its client_id.
  • It MUST contain an Audience naming the authorization server, and the server MUST reject any assertion that lacks its own identity there.
  • It MUST contain an Expires At time. The server MUST reject expired assertions, allowing for clock skew, and may reject ones that expire unreasonably far ahead.
  • It MAY contain an Issued At time. Times are REQUIRED to be UTC with no time zone component.
  • The server MUST reject an invalid signature or MAC.

An Assertion ID is a nonce or unique identifier that can be used to de-duplicate one-time-use assertions. Issuer and Audience values are compared with the Simple String Comparison method of RFC 3986 unless a profile says otherwise.
sections.eli5: A good note names who wrote it, who it is about, who may read it, and when it stops working. The front desk throws away notes with a forged signature or an old date.

sections.title: Common Scenarios
sections.content:
The RFC walks through how the pieces combine.

  • Client authentication: the client sends client_assertion_type and client_assertion. The Subject identifies the client, and for a self-issued assertion the Issuer does too.
  • Client acting for itself: this works like the Client Credentials Grant. The request uses assertion client authentication with grant_type=client_credentials.
  • Client acting for a user: the request uses grant_type and assertion. The Subject identifies the authorized accessor, typically the resource owner or a delegate.
  • Anonymous user: the Subject is an agreed value, such as an opaque pseudonymous identifier or a static value like anonymous. Authorization can rest on claims in the assertion. The RFC's example is an assertion from a trusted issuer that the bearer is over 18.
sections.eli5: You can show the desk a note for yourself, a note that says you are acting for a grown-up, or a note that only says "this person is over 18" without giving a name.

sections.title: Why a Profile Is Needed
sections.content:
The RFC states that, on its own, it is not enough to build interoperable implementations, because it leaves the data formats of many values undefined. Two profiles fill the gap: RFC 7522 for SAML 2.0 assertions and RFC 7523 for JSON Web Tokens.

Even with a profile, the parties must agree on several things out of band: the Issuer and Audience values, supported assertion and client authentication types, the token endpoint location, the key used to sign and verify, one-time-use restrictions, the maximum assertion lifetime and the Subject and attribute requirements. The exchange of that information is explicitly out of scope.
sections.eli5: The rules say how letters get handed over, but not what language they are written in. Each school still has to agree on the language and on who may sign.

sections.title: Security and Privacy
sections.content:
The RFC lists three threats and their countermeasures.

  • Forged assertion: an attacker alters or forges an assertion. The answer is integrity protection, meaning the issuer signs it or computes a MAC.
  • Stolen assertion: an attacker eavesdrops and replays it later. The main mitigation is secure channels with server authentication. Servers can also combine the Assertion ID with the Issued At and Expires At times: reject already-seen IDs, and the validity window means the server need not keep an infinite table of IDs.
  • Disclosure of personal information: TLS keeps eavesdroppers out, and some formats allow encryption so the client cannot read the content. Where a token service put attributes in the assertion, prior consent from the resource owner should be obtained, though OAuth does not itself provide that.

On privacy, deployments should include only the minimum information needed. The Subject can be an anonymous or pseudonymous value.
sections.eli5: Someone could fake a note or steal one and use it again later. The desk checks the signature, the date and whether it has seen that note before, and notes should only be passed around in sealed envelopes.

sections.title: IANA Registrations
sections.content:
The RFC registers three parameter names in the IANA "OAuth Parameters" registry established by RFC 6749: assertion, client_assertion and client_assertion_type. Each has the usage location "token request" and the IESG as change controller.

It does not register the URN values itself. It suggests URNs of the form urn:ietf:params:oauth:grant-type:* for grant types and urn:ietf:params:oauth:client-assertion-type:* for client assertion types, to be requested using the template in RFC 6755.
sections.eli5: The three new form boxes get written in the official list of box names, so nobody else uses the same names for something different.

data.title: Token request with an assertion grant
data.code:
POST /token HTTP/1.1
Host: server.example.com
Content-Type: application/x-www-form-urlencoded

grant_type=urn%3Aietf%3Aparams%3Aoauth%3Agrant-type%3Asaml2-bearer&
assertion=PHNhbWxwOl...[omitted for brevity]...ZT4

items.title: Issuer
items.text: Who issued and signed the assertion. MUST be present.

items.title: Subject
items.text: Who the assertion is about. MUST be present.

items.title: Audience
items.text: Who may process it. MUST name the authorization server.

items.title: Expires At
items.text: When it stops being valid. MUST be present.

items.title: Issued At
items.text: When it was issued. MAY be present.

items.title: Assertion ID
items.text: A unique identifier for de-duplicating one-time-use assertions.
